title: Share Buyback
subtitle: A way to pay shareholders that isn't a dividend
openingQuestion: How does a 10% share buyback affect EPS?
openingOptions: It depends entirely on the purchase price that was paid
EPS rises ~11% because shares outstanding fall 10%
explanation: A share buyback is a way to return money to shareholders instead of a dividend: shares outstanding fall, so each remaining shareholder's slice grows. Its advantage over a dividend is flexibility - pausing it isn't read as a bad signal. But it's fundamentally an investment decision: the company is buying itself, so it creates value when the stock is undervalued and destroys value when bought at a high price.

diagram.label: The same profit divided by fewer shares

realWorldExample.description: Apple bought back hundreds of billions of USD in stock from 2012-2023, reducing shares outstanding from ~26B to ~15.5B. EPS rose sharply even though net income grew only modestly. Warren Buffett strongly supports this policy.

quiz.question: When does a buyback create value for shareholders?
options: When a business borrows to fund the buyback
When buying at an all-time-high price
When a business needs to push EPS up to hit a target
When buying at a price below the stock's intrinsic value
quiz.explanation: Buybacks create value when buying below intrinsic value. Buying overvalued = destroying value (spending real cash on something expensive). Managers can use buybacks to game EPS rather than benefit shareholders - the two need to be distinguished.

quiz.question: Why do many investors, including Warren Buffett, favor share buybacks over dividend increases in some cases, even though both return cash to shareholders?
options: Because a buyback is flexible and doesn't create a fixed expectation for future years
Because buybacks are always tax-free while dividends are taxed
Because buybacks increase equity on the balance sheet
Because buybacks guarantee the share price won't fall long-term
quiz.explanation: Buybacks have a flexibility advantage and sometimes a tax advantage, but they only truly create value when a company buys back shares at a REASONABLE price or below fair value - if management buys back shares when they're overvalued, that's actually destroying value.

quiz.question: Profit of 500 billion, 100 million shares. Buying back 10 million shares, how does EPS change?
options: From 5,000 to exactly 5,500, up 10%
From 5,000 to about 5,556, i.e. up 11%
From 5,000 down to 4,500 because cash on hand fell
Unchanged because net income stays at 500 billion
quiz.explanation: EPS = 500 billion / 90 million = 5,556. A 10% reduction in share count raises EPS by 11%, not 10% - because the denominator shrinks proportionally. No additional profit was created.

quiz.question: Why doesn't a rising EPS after a buyback automatically mean shareholders got richer?
options: Because the repurchased shares get reissued later
Because EPS growth always brings the P/E down so price stays flat
Because the company spent real cash to buy, and assets fell correspondingly
Because shareholders must pay tax on the increased EPS each year
quiz.explanation: The pie is split among fewer people, but the pie also shrank by exactly the amount spent. Shareholders only truly benefit if the purchase price was below fair value - otherwise it's just a different way to divide the same thing.

quiz.question: Management with a bonus tied to EPS decides on a large buyback. What should you watch for?
options: Minority shareholders will be forced to sell their shares
The buyback will breach a loan covenant
Treasury shares must be cancelled within one year
Personal incentives may override shareholder interests
quiz.explanation: A buyback pushes EPS up without needing to run the business better, making it the cheapest way to hit a bonus target. When reading a buyback program, always check the purchase price against fair value, and the compensation structure of the person making the decision.

keyTakeaways: Buyback = reduce shares outstanding → EPS rises
More flexible than a dividend - doesn't create a fixed expectation
Only creates value when buying below intrinsic value

practicePrompt.question: A company has Net Income = 500 billion, 100 million shares outstanding (EPS = 5,000 VND/share). The company spends 200 billion in cash to buy back 10 million shares, reducing shares outstanding to 90 million. What is the new EPS after the buyback, and why does it change?
options: EPS rises: 500 billion / 90 million ≈ 5,556 dong, because the very same profit is now split across far fewer shares
EPS is unchanged because a buyback doesn't affect the company's Net Income
EPS falls to 4,500 VND/share because the company spent 200 billion in cash to buy back shares
EPS only changes if the company simultaneously increases Net Income; a buyback alone isn't enough to affect EPS
practicePrompt.explanation: Buyback = reduce shares outstanding → EPS rises. Because Net Income (500 billion) is unchanged but shares outstanding fell (100m → 90m), EPS = 500/90 ≈ 5,556, higher than the original 5,000 - this is why many companies use buybacks as a way to 'lift' EPS and return value to remaining shareholders.

summary.keyIdea: Buyback = reduce shares outstanding → EPS rises
summary.commonMistake: Reading the concept as a phrase to memorize rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: More flexible than a dividend - doesn't create a fixed expectation

application.title: Apply it now
application.message: Think of something you spend 'flexibly without commitment' (a treat for yourself, a spontaneous gift) versus a 'fixed committed' expense (regular savings) - which is more like a dividend, and which is more like a buyback?
application.secondary: Understanding this difference helps you read corporate financial reports with a clearer eye.

sections.text: A share buyback is the second way to return money to shareholders, alongside dividends - but instead of transferring cash directly, the company uses cash to buy back its own shares on the market, reducing the number of shares outstanding.
The mechanism: how a buyback raises EPS

When the number of shares outstanding falls, the same net profit is now divided among fewer shares, raising EPS (earnings per share) even though absolute profit hasn't changed. Apple is a classic example: from 2012-2023, Apple bought back hundreds of billions of USD in stock, reducing shares outstanding from about 26 billion to about 15.5 billion shares - EPS rose sharply even though net income grew only modestly. Warren Buffett is a strong supporter of this strategy when executed properly.
When a buyback actually creates value

A buyback only creates value for shareholders when the company buys back shares at a price below or equal to intrinsic value - similar to buying an asset at a bargain. If management buys back shares when they're overvalued, that's effectively spending shareholders' cash on something expensive, destroying value for the remaining shareholders. Some managers use buybacks purely to 'juice' short-term EPS (EPS gaming) rather than for shareholders' genuine benefit - investors need to distinguish between these two motives.

left.label: Dividend
left.text: A committed periodic payment, creates a stable expectation, taxed immediately upon receipt (in many markets), hard to cut without a negative reaction.

right.label: Buyback
right.text: Flexible, doesn't create a repeated commitment, has a tax advantage in many markets (only taxed when the shares are sold), but only creates value when bought at a reasonable price or below intrinsic value.

items: A buyback reduces shares outstanding → EPS rises even though net income is unchanged
More flexible than a dividend because it doesn't create a repeated expectation each period
Only creates real value when buying below intrinsic value - buying when overvalued destroys value

lines: A buyback isn't automatically 'good' or 'bad' - always ask: at what price relative to fair value is the company buying back its shares?
